summary: Extends HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery so a location request can identify the device, not rely only on the source IP address. This helps where the address does not map directly to a device's location. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Instead of finding where you are by the address on the envelope, you can say who you are, so the location service can find the right place.

subtitle: Lets a HELD location request name the device it is about, instead of relying only on the sender's IP address.

tldr.problem: A HELD location server normally uses the request's source IP address to decide whose location to return, which fails when more than an IP address is needed or when someone other than the device asks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a device element, with identifiers such as IP, MAC, NAI, URI and cellular numbers, that can be put in the body of a HELD location request, plus a badIdentifier error and a requiredIdentifiers element.
tldr.outcome: Requests that carry identifiers are not treated as location configuration protocol requests unless spoofing is prevented. Third-party requests must be authenticated and explicitly authorized.

today: RFC 6155 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6915. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Beyond the Source IP Address
sections.content:
In HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD, RFC 5985), a Location Information Server (LIS) normally uses the source IP address of a locationRequest as a pointer to the location determination process. That works where a device's location can be determined from its IP address.

This RFC addresses two further cases. In the first, location configuration needs identifiers other than, or in addition to, the source IP address. In the second, an entity other than the device asks for the device's location. It extends HELD so the request body can carry device identifiers, defined by an XML schema.

HELD with these extensions is explicitly not considered a Location Configuration Protocol (LCP). An LCP is limited to the exchange between a device and its LIS and can vouch for the device's identity through the packet's source address and return routability. With identifiers in the body, the request may come from a third party, so extra authorization is needed.

When device identity is present, the source IP address is not used to identify the subject of the request.
sections.eli5: Normally the location helper looks at the return address on your envelope. Now you can also write on the letter whose location you want to know.

sections.title: When an Identifier Is Suitable
sections.content:
An identifier MUST only be allowed if it identifies a single device at the time location is determined. The LIS is responsible for making sure the identifier is uniquely attributable to that device. Transient or ambiguous identifiers could be used by an attacker to learn about another device or to trick the LIS into giving misleading answers.

  • Subjective network views. An identifier may mean different things in different network contexts. Network address translation and private-use addresses are typical causes. A LIS can be configured to account for the requestor's view or reject such requests.
  • Transient identifiers. If an identifier is reassigned between the time a request is made and when it is received, the LIS would locate the wrong entity. A LIS must not provide location if the identifier might refer to a different device.
  • Interfaces and devices. Many identifiers name a network interface. Identifying any one interface is assumed to be enough to identify the device, but an interface can be physically separable from it.
sections.eli5: A name only works if it points to exactly one person. If two kids share the nickname, or the nickname changes hands, the helper could look for the wrong child.

sections.title: Identifier Format and Protocol Details
sections.content:
Identity is expressed in XML. The device element is a general container that goes inside a HELD request. The namespace for these elements is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:geopriv:held:id.

A LIS that supports this specification echoes the device element in a successful response, listing the identifiers used. If the echo is absent, the location was generated from the source IP address in the request.

A new HELD error code, badIdentifier, means the requestor is not authorized to use that identifier, or the identifier is badly formatted or not supported by the LIS. If the LIS needs identifiers that were not supplied, the error response MAY include a requiredIdentifiers element listing the XML qualified names of the elements it needs.
sections.eli5: The request now has a place to write who you mean. If the helper needs more details, it can answer with a list of what to add.

sections.title: The Defined Identifiers
sections.content:
The device schema accepts elements from any namespace, so other identifiers can be defined later. This RFC defines a basic set.

  • ip: an IPv4 or IPv6 address, with a v attribute giving the version.
  • mac: a MAC-48, EUI-48 or EUI-64 address. A locally assigned address can only be used within its administrative domain.
  • udpport, tcpport, sctpport, dccpport: a port number, useful with an IP address to pick out a device behind a NAT in some cases.
  • nai: a Network Access Identifier, with a backslash-and-two-hex-digits escape for octets that are not valid UTF-8.
  • uri: any URI that requestor and LIS understand the same way, including a tel: URI. Care is needed because a URI may resolve to several destinations.
  • fqdn: a fully qualified domain name. It is not suitable if the name does not correspond to a single IP address or host.
  • Cellular identifiers: msisdn, imsi, imei, min, mdn.
  • duid: a DHCP Unique Identifier, written in hexadecimal.

For WiMAX networks, an NAI is uniquely attributable to one device, and an IP address alone is not enough for the LIS to locate it. The LIS asks the AAA server about the NAI, using a message that carries an MS-Identity-Assertion parameter. If the AAA server returns an IP address matching the request's source address, the request can be authorized under the LCP policy. Otherwise it is treated as a third-party request. The AAA server MUST be authenticated and the AAA protocol MUST protect against modification and replay.
sections.eli5: You can point at someone by their house number, their phone number, their school ID or their username. Each kind of label has its own rules about when it is good enough.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Location configuration protocols use an authorization model called the LCP policy: the only authorized recipient of a target's location is the target. Once identifiers are in the request body, HELD is no longer an LCP in the strict sense, and the LIS needs authorization rules provisioned by one or more Rule Makers.

When a target asks for its own location with these extensions, return routability alone no longer protects against spoofing, so specific measures MUST be defined for the alternative identifier. This document defines them for an NAI in WiMAX networks and for no other identifier. The RFC warns that credentials can be shared: if devices with different MAC addresses use the same NAI concurrently, the NAI cannot be used to give a target its own location. Unauthenticated MAC addresses supplied alongside an authenticated NAI should not be trusted either.

A LIS that accepts third-party requests acts as a Location Server. It MUST explicitly authorize requests under policies from Rule Makers, including the target, and MUST authenticate requestors. Until a policy exists, the LIS MUST reject third-party requests; the default is deny all.
sections.eli5: Normally you may only ask where you yourself are. If a friend wants to ask, there must be a clear permission slip first. With no slip, the answer is no.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The TLS-based protections from RFC 5985 for server authentication, confidentiality and integrity apply to both target and third-party requests. All HELD requests containing identity MUST be authenticated by the LIS. It is RECOMMENDED that authentication give at least the assurance of the return reachability that HELD gets from a completed TCP handshake. Requestors MUST support HTTP digest authentication for requests that include device identity. An unauthenticated request with device identity can be challenged with HTTP 401 or rejected with HTTP 403, and a LIS SHOULD NOT send a 401 if the device does not include identity.

Transient identifiers allow an attack if an identifier is reassigned between authorization and the location answer. Ambiguous identifiers let an attacker who legitimately gains authorization for one device get location for every device the identifier might name. Identity information from a device is private data, so the LIS MUST NOT use it for any purpose other than serving that request. Third-party requests MUST be explicitly authorized by a policy established by a Rule Maker.
sections.eli5: The helper must check who is asking, and it must not reuse the details you gave for anything else.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:geopriv:held:id and the XML schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:geopriv:held:id, following the guidelines of RFC 3688. The schema itself is Section 6 of the document.

It also registers the badIdentifier error code in the HELD Error Codes sub-registry. The code means that a device identifier in the request was not supported by the LIS, was badly formatted, or was not one the requestor was authorized to use.
sections.eli5: The new labels and the new error message are entered in the official list so everyone uses them the same way.

data.title: Request carrying an IPv4 device identifier
badIdentifier error with requiredIdentifiers
data.code:
<error xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:geopriv:held"
       code="badIdentifier">
  <message xml:lang="en">MAC address required</message>
  <requiredIdentifiers
      xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:geopriv:held:id">
    mac ip
  </requiredIdentifiers>
</error>

items.label: MSISDN
items.desc: An E.164 number between 6 and 15 digits long.

items.label: IMSI
items.desc: Subscriber identity for GSM and UMTS, 6 to 15 digits.

items.label: IMEI
items.desc: Unique device serial number, up to 15 digits.

items.label: MDN
items.desc: An E.164 number, used similarly to MSISDN.
